name: Chloe Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Chloe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Can you describe a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push coal with a dozer on the stockpile at an open-cut coal mine, shaping the piles so the reclaimer can load the trains. Twelve-hour days, four on, four off. I ran a hair salon on Station Street for twenty-eight years, sold it when the rent doubled, and Tom, my husband, who's a diesel mechanic here, said they were hiring. So at fifty-six I went from scissors to a forty-tonne dozer.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Harder than I let on. I'm still the worst on my crew at keeping the pile even, and the trainer, Graham, has the patience of a saint. But I like the cab, the radio on, nobody asking me to make them look like a film star. I'm not a gadget person; I've got a flip phone and I'm proud of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a lot of fuss over nothing, isn't it. At break I'd probably say the computers were never going to push coal anyway. I don't go online, so that's the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get my eight or nine years and then I stop. The only thing that worries me about the mine is coal itself, whether the power stations keep buying it. AI's not really on my list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep learning the dozer, get signed off on the stockpile without Graham riding along, and keep putting a bit away. Tom and I want the house fully paid before I turn sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said coal itself worries you more than AI. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine's got a closure date that keeps moving, 2038 last I heard. Everybody in town talks about that, not robots. When I sold the salon, it wasn't technology that got me, it was the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets saved each month at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred, after the house payment. We've got maybe three months in the bank. It's not a fortune, but it's more than I ever had with the salon.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss over nothing, and that computers were never going to push coal. She doesn't go online, so that would be the end of it.
S0.think: She expects to get her eight or nine years and then stop. Her real worry about the mine is whether power stations keep buying coal, not AI.
S0.do: Keeps learning the dozer until she can work the stockpile without a trainer. Keeps saving about four hundred a month so the house is paid off before she's sixty-five.
S0.feel: Calm; it's the world she already knows.
S0.quote: When I sold the salon, it wasn't technology that got me, it was the landlord.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is matter-of-fact and proudly low-tech. Her sense of risk is shaped by the coal mine's closure date and her own past with a landlord, not by AI. She's open about still being the weakest operator on her crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just business, things change, always have. I'm not one to march about it. But I'd say the company owes the older workers a fair go, because we came here in good faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me nervous. I'm new and I'm slow, so if they bring in self-driving dozers on the stockpile, I'm first out the gate. And I'm not going to learn computers at fifty-eight; I'd be useless at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back now, no new car, no cruise with my sister. I'd start cutting hair from home again on my days off, just regulars, to bring in a bit on the side. And I'd wait and see what the company actually does before I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the landlord rang and said we need to talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cutting hair rather than learning the new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good at hair and I'm bad at screens. Thirty years of hands, you don't lose that. A robot isn't going to do Mrs Patel's perm the way she likes it, not in a few years anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom fixes the trucks. If they go driverless, they'll still need fixing, so I think he's safer than me. That makes me feel better and worse at the same time, if that makes sense.

S1.say: I'd say it's just business and things always change, and she isn't one to march. But the company owes older workers a fair go because they came in good faith.
S1.think: She's nervous that as the newest and slowest operator she'd be the first to go if self-driving dozers arrive. She won't learn computers at fifty-eight and thinks she'd be useless at it.
S1.do: Cancels the new car and the cruise with her sister. Starts cutting hair at home for regulars on days off, and waits to see what the company actually does.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the landlord ringing to say "we need to talk".
S1.quote: A robot isn't going to do Mrs Patel's perm the way she likes it, not in a few years anyway.
S1.fieldNote: Her answer to change is to fall back on a skill she trusts, hairdressing, rather than learn something new. She doesn't blame anyone, calling it "just business". The mixed feeling about Tom being safer than her was a nice honest moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there's nothing any of us can do about it, so let's look after each other. I wouldn't be pointing fingers. I'd be asking what the company plans for its people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it's both of us out at once, me and Tom. If robots can fix trucks too, his safe job isn't safe. We'd be two people near sixty with three months of savings and a house not paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't the house payment, power and food, from the first week. I'd go and see the bank about stretching the loan out if we had to. I'd ask our son if we could count on him for a few months if it came to that, which I'd hate, and I'd cut hair for anyone who'd pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep. I'd be up making tea at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son when you asked him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is only for a bit, love, until we sort ourselves out. He'd say yes, he always does. But I'd remember sitting in my own mother's kitchen asking her for money when the salon was struggling, and I swore I'd never put my kids through that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the hairdressing still feel like a fallback here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less so. If the robots can do anything, maybe they'll do hair too. But people want a chat with their haircut, and I'm betting a few of my old ladies will stick with me while it lasts.

S2.say: I'd say there's nothing any of us can do, so let's look after each other, without pointing fingers. She'd ask what the company plans for its people.
S2.think: She thinks she and Tom would both be out at once, because robots that can fix trucks would take his job too. They'd be nearly sixty with three months of savings and an unpaid house.
S2.do: Cuts spending to the house payment, power and food from the first week and asks the bank about stretching the loan. Asks her son for help if needed and cuts hair for anyone who'll pay.
S2.feel: Alarmed, unable to sleep, making tea at three in the morning.
S2.quote: We'd be two people near sixty with three months of savings and a house not paid off.
S2.fieldNote: What tips her into alarm is losing both incomes at once. Even here she doesn't blame anyone; she just tightens up and looks after the household. Asking her son for help clearly hurts her pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, at least. People can get their affairs in order. I'd tell the young ones to keep their eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three by 2031. If I can hold on until then, the house would be nearly done and Tom and I could manage on less. But I'm the junior, so holding on isn't up to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, every dollar from overtime and the hair, to get to six months or more. We'd pay extra off the house, maybe two hundred a month. I'd build up my hairdressing regulars so there's something there when the mine finishes with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a way through. It's like getting the salon ready to sell: hard, but there's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I know people expect me to say yes, but I'd rather use the time to do more of what I'm already good at. Some of us aren't built for starting over twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pub dinners on a Friday, sadly. And the caravan trips. Tom would grumble but he'd understand.

S3.say: I'd say five years at least lets people get their affairs in order. She'd tell the young ones to keep their eyes open.
S3.think: At sixty-three by 2031, she'd be close to having the house paid and could manage on less. But as the junior, whether she holds on isn't up to her.
S3.do: Saves overtime and hair money to reach six months or more and pays an extra two hundred a month off the house. Builds up her hairdressing regulars for when the mine lets her go.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to see a way through, like getting the salon ready to sell.
S3.quote: Some of us aren't built for starting over twice.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Chloe makes a practical plan built on saving and her old trade rather than retraining. She's clear and unapologetic that she won't learn new technology. The comparison with selling her salon shows she's been through hard change before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and it's not something I'd lose sleep over. Maybe the young ones should start planning. I'd say that on my break and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight. I'd have planned to stop at sixty-five or sixty-six anyway. So really it's my kids' problem, not mine, as long as the mine keeps me on that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the dozer, keep saving, and get the house done. Maybe I'd keep a few hair clients as a hobby. I wouldn't change much at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little niggle about whether they'd keep me till sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the niggle exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That they'd start bringing robots in bit by bit before the end date, and the junior people would go first. Ten years to the finish line doesn't mean ten years before they start trimming. I've seen how things go quiet before the big announcement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter, who's a bookkeeper, to think hard about it. She does numbers on a computer all day, and that sounds like exactly the kind of thing these machines would do first.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time and not something she'd lose sleep over. She'd tell the young ones to start planning and leave it there.
S4.think: She'd be sixty-eight by then and planned to stop at sixty-five or sixty-six anyway. It's her children's problem more than hers, if the mine keeps her on that long.
S4.do: Carries on with the dozer, keeps saving and pays off the house. Keeps a few hair clients as a hobby and changes very little.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a niggle about whether the mine keeps her until sixty-five.
S4.quote: Ten years to the finish line doesn't mean ten years before they start trimming.
S4.fieldNote: She says she wouldn't lose sleep, yet the follow-up revealed a real worry about early cuts for junior staff. That gap puts her at uneasy rather than calm. Her concern for her bookkeeper daughter was sharp and specific.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Tom and I would both be out at once. What would help is the company giving older workers a decent payout and a bit of notice, and some kind of help with the house loan so we don't lose the roof.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. It's the people, really. Same as the salon. I'd miss Graham's terrible jokes on the radio more than I'd miss the wages.

headlineQuote: I'd miss Graham's terrible jokes on the radio more than I'd miss the wages.
portrait: Chloe Weber is a fifty-eight-year-old former salon owner who now pushes coal with a dozer on the stockpile at an open-cut coal mine, where her husband Tom is a diesel mechanic. She's practical, middle-of-the-road, owns a flip phone and won't learn new technology, falling back on her hairdressing skills instead. She's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, but AGI in two years alarms her because it could take both her job and Tom's. With five or ten years she saves hard, pays down the house and counts on retiring before the robots reach her.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because she and Tom could lose both incomes at once with the house not yet paid off.
whatWouldHelp: A decent payout and notice for older workers, plus help with the house loan so they don't lose their home.
